title: AP Latin
summary: Read Latin syntax and develop evidence-based interpretations alongside the current Pliny and Vergil sequence.
frameworkNote: Checked on 15 October 2026 against the six-unit framework revised for 2025-26 and current in 2026-27. It includes Pliny, Vergil, teacher-selected texts and an annual course project. All Latin sentences here are original teaching examples, not quotations from required texts. Study the assigned passages and current project materials with your teacher.

modules.title: Build a sentence from its inflections
modules.focus: Unit 1 prose: identify relationships before translating.
explanation: Latin word order is flexible because endings carry much of the grammatical information. Identify the finite verb, then look for a subject that agrees in number and a direct object in the accusative when the verb takes one. Case forms can be ambiguous, so use syntax and meaning together.

A translation should preserve relationships without mechanically copying Latin order. In “puellam poeta laudat”, puellam is accusative and poeta is nominative: the poet praises the girl. Poeta is a first-declension noun referring here to a male poet; a noun’s ending alone does not settle its natural gender.

workedExample.prompt: Translate the original sentence “servum domina vocat”.
steps: Identify vocat as “calls” and domina as the nominative subject.
Identify servum as the accusative object: “The mistress calls the enslaved man.”

misconception.claim: The first Latin word is always the subject.
misconception.correction: Case and syntax determine grammatical roles; position can instead contribute emphasis.

questions.prompt: Translate “agricolam puer videt”.
questions.answer: The boy sees the farmer.
checkpoints: Makes puer the subject
Makes agricolam the object

questions.prompt: What should you do when a case ending is ambiguous?
questions.hint: Use more than a dictionary gloss.
questions.answer: Check the verb, agreement and surrounding construction before deciding the word’s function.
checkpoints: Uses syntax
Checks agreement

questions.prompt: Translate the original sentence 'nauta pueris aquam portat'.
questions.hint: Find portat and its singular subject.
hints: Find portat and its singular subject.
questions.answer: The sailor carries water to or for the boys. Nauta is the nominative subject and aquam the accusative object. Pueris is the dative recipient in this reading.
checkpoints: The sailor carries water to or for the boys.
Nauta is the nominative subject and aquam the accusative object.
Pueris is the dative recipient in this reading.

questions.prompt: Why cannot puellae always be translated 'the girls'?
questions.answer: Puellae may be nominative plural, genitive singular or dative singular. The ending alone does not settle its role. The verb and surrounding construction determine the appropriate reading.
checkpoints: Puellae may be nominative plural, genitive singular or dative singular.
The ending alone does not settle its role.
The verb and surrounding construction determine the appropriate reading.

notes.title: Build a sentence from its inflections in depth
paragraphs: Begin a Latin sentence by identifying the finite verb's person and number, then test candidate subjects against it. A noun's case ending can have more than one possible analysis, so agreement and the verb's construction must work together. The nominative commonly identifies the subject and the accusative a direct object, but a preposition may also govern an accusative. Adjectives agree in case, number and gender, not necessarily in identical endings. Translate the relationships into natural English only after the Latin structure is secure; English word order should not decide who acts.

workedExamples.prompt: Translate the original practice sentence 'puellae librum magistro dant'.
steps: Dant is third-person plural, 'they give'; puellae can supply the nominative plural subject.
Librum is the accusative object and magistro the dative recipient.
workedExamples.conclusion: 'The girls give a book to the teacher.'

flashcards.front: Must agreeing adjectives have identical endings?
flashcards.back: No; they agree in case, number and gender.

diagrams.title: Giving a book
diagrams.description: Inflections distinguish agent, object and recipient.

modules.title: Trace viewpoint in an event narrative
modules.focus: Unit 2 Pliny context: distinguish observation, report and sequence.
explanation: An eyewitness narrative can combine what a writer saw, what others reported and what the writer later inferred. Identify the grammatical signals of each layer before discussing reliability. A vivid account is still a constructed narrative with a recipient, purpose and selected details.

Latin indirect statement commonly uses an accusative subject and infinitive after a verb of saying or thinking. In the original example “dicit nautam venire”, nautam is the subject of venire: “He says that the sailor is coming.” The infinitive’s tense expresses time relative to the reporting verb.

workedExample.prompt: Translate “dixit amicos advenisse”, an original practice sentence.
steps: Dixit introduces reported speech; amicos is the accusative subject.
Advenisse is a perfect infinitive, so the arrival precedes the saying: “He said that the friends had arrived.”

misconception.claim: A perfect infinitive always refers directly to the present speaker’s past.
misconception.correction: Its time is normally understood relative to the main reporting verb.

questions.prompt: Translate “credit urbem tutam esse”.
questions.hint: Treat urbem as the indirect statement’s subject.
questions.answer: He or she believes that the city is safe.
checkpoints: Identifies indirect statement
Preserves the state of safety

questions.prompt: What evidence separates observation from hearsay in analysis?
questions.answer: A verb identifying what someone said or reported marks a different evidential layer from the narrator’s direct observation.
checkpoints: Names a textual signal
Limits the reliability claim

questions.prompt: Translate the original 'putat puerum discessisse'.
questions.answer: He or she thinks that the boy has departed. Puerum is the reported subject. Discessisse places departure before the thinking.
checkpoints: He or she thinks that the boy has departed.
Puerum is the reported subject.
Discessisse places departure before the thinking.

questions.prompt: Contrast 'dixit amicum venire' with 'dixit amicum venisse'.
questions.answer: The first says the friend was coming at the time of the report. The second says the friend had come earlier. The infinitive expresses relative time, not a change in the reporting verb.
checkpoints: The first says the friend was coming at the time of the report.
The second says the friend had come earlier.
The infinitive expresses relative time, not a change in the reporting verb.

notes.title: Trace viewpoint in an event narrative in depth
paragraphs: Indirect statement commonly makes the reported subject accusative and uses an infinitive. The infinitive's tense is relative to the reporting verb: present for contemporaneous action, perfect for earlier action and future for later action. Thus a past reporting verb does not make a present infinitive express a prior event. Distinguish what the narrator asserts from what a named speaker reports. A statement may be grammatically clear while its truth remains contested within the narrative. Accurate translation preserves the attribution instead of silently treating every reported claim as the narrator's verified observation.

workedExamples.prompt: Translate the original sentence 'nuntius dixit milites pontem custodire'.
steps: Dixit supplies the past reporting action; milites is the accusative subject of custodire.
The present infinitive makes guarding contemporaneous with the report.
workedExamples.conclusion: 'The messenger said that the soldiers were guarding the bridge.'

flashcards.front: What is milites in the reported clause?
What time does a present infinitive express?
flashcards.back: Time contemporaneous with the reporting verb.

flashcards.front: Does reported speech prove its claim true?
flashcards.back: No; attribution remains part of the meaning.

diagrams.title: Two levels of narration
diagrams.description: The report and its content remain distinct.

modules.title: Read purpose and social relationship
modules.focus: Unit 3 letters: connect syntax, recipient and tone.
explanation: A letter addresses a particular recipient and may request, reassure, justify or advise. Tone arises from the combination of vocabulary, sentence structure and social relationship. Do not assume that a private-sounding letter has no concern for later readers.

A purpose clause with ut commonly takes the subjunctive. In “epistulam scripsit ut amicum moneret”, the imperfect subjunctive moneret follows a past main verb and gives the aim: “He wrote a letter to warn his friend.” Purpose describes intention, not proof that the friend was successfully warned.

workedExample.prompt: Translate the original sentence “venit ut auxilium peteret”.
steps: Identify venit as “he came” in this context and peteret as imperfect subjunctive.
Translate ut as purpose: “He came to ask for help.” Do not turn the purpose into an achieved result.

misconception.claim: An ut clause always gives the same relationship.
misconception.correction: Purpose and result clauses must be distinguished through syntax and context.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose in “misit nuntium ut cives moneret” ?
questions.answer: He sent a messenger to warn the citizens.
checkpoints: Identifies warning as the aim
Does not assert the citizens obeyed

questions.prompt: Why consider a letter’s recipient when analysing tone?
questions.answer: A request to an official and reassurance to a close relation may use different strategies even on a similar topic.
checkpoints: Connects audience to choices
Avoids treating tone as isolated vocabulary

questions.prompt: Translate the original 'legatos mittit ut pacem petant'.
questions.answer: He or she sends envoys to seek peace. Petant is present subjunctive after a present main verb. The sentence does not say peace was obtained.
checkpoints: He or she sends envoys to seek peace.
Petant is present subjunctive after a present main verb.
The sentence does not say peace was obtained.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between purpose and outcome in a letter requesting help.
questions.answer: A request can explain why the writer sent the letter. It does not establish that the recipient acted. A later response or narrated event is needed to support that outcome.
checkpoints: A request can explain why the writer sent the letter.
It does not establish that the recipient acted.
A later response or narrated event is needed to support that outcome.

notes.title: Read purpose and social relationship in depth
paragraphs: A purpose clause explains an intended aim and normally uses the subjunctive with ut, or ne for a negative purpose. Sequence of tenses often places a present subjunctive after a primary-tense main verb and an imperfect subjunctive after a historical-tense main verb. This pattern helps organise the sentence but does not prove that the intention succeeded. In a letter, requests and reassurances also depend on the writer's relationship to the recipient. A polite or affectionate tone may serve persuasion as well as express feeling, so connect interpretation to specific language.

workedExamples.prompt: Translate the original sentence 'ianuam clausit ne canis exiret'.
steps: Clausit is a completed closing; ne introduces a negative purpose.
Exiret is imperfect subjunctive, aligned with the historical main verb.
workedExamples.conclusion: 'He or she closed the door so that the dog would not go out.' The dog's eventual behaviour is not stated.

flashcards.front: Does a purpose clause establish success?

diagrams.title: Preventing an exit
diagrams.description: The construction separates action and intended consequence.

nodes.label: Dog remaining inside
nodes.detail: The intended result, not a confirmed outcome.

modules.title: Read poetry through syntax and metre
modules.focus: Unit 4 poetry: distinguish word placement from grammatical connection.
explanation: Latin poetry can separate words that belong together. Agreement in case, number and gender helps connect an adjective to its noun across intervening words. Translate the grammatical relationship first, then ask how the separation directs attention or creates emphasis.

Dactylic hexameter organises syllable quantities into six feet. A dactyl contains one long and two short syllables; a spondee contains two long syllables. Quantity is not identical to English stress. Accurate scansion also requires attention to vowel length, syllable closure and elision in the actual assigned verse.

workedExample.prompt: Interpret the original prose-order variation “magnam poeta narrat cladem”.
steps: Connect magnam to cladem through feminine accusative singular agreement.
Translate “The poet recounts a great disaster”; then describe how separation delays completion of the noun phrase.

misconception.claim: Poetic word order makes case endings optional.
misconception.correction: Inflection remains essential for connecting separated words.

questions.prompt: Represent a dactyl using long and short labels.
questions.answer: Long-short-short.
checkpoints: Begins with a long
Ends with two shorts

questions.prompt: What links “saeva” and “ira” if other words intervene?
questions.answer: Their matching feminine nominative singular forms can identify the adjective-noun relationship, subject to the full sentence.
checkpoints: Uses agreement
Checks context

questions.prompt: Analyse the original 'longam puella narrat fabulam'.
questions.answer: Longam agrees with fabulam in feminine accusative singular. Puella is the subject of narrat. The girl tells a long story.
checkpoints: Longam agrees with fabulam in feminine accusative singular.
Puella is the subject of narrat.
The girl tells a long story.

questions.prompt: Why is counting six written words not a method for identifying hexameter?
questions.answer: Hexameter has six metrical feet, not six words. Syllable quantities determine the pattern. Word boundaries need not coincide with foot boundaries.
checkpoints: Hexameter has six metrical feet, not six words.
Syllable quantities determine the pattern.
Word boundaries need not coincide with foot boundaries.

notes.title: Read poetry through syntax and metre in depth
paragraphs: Poetic word order can separate an adjective from its noun while preserving agreement. Identify the grammatical unit before interpreting the delay or emphasis caused by separation. Syllable quantity, which structures classical hexameter, differs from stress: a long syllable can arise through a long vowel or through its consonantal environment. A dactyl has a long followed by two shorts, and a spondee two longs. Scansion needs the actual words, vowel quantities and elision rules; naming a metre is not evidence that an invented prose sentence fits it.

workedExamples.prompt: Analyse the original prose sentence 'alta per silvas resonat vox'; no metrical claim is made.
steps: Alta agrees with vox, feminine nominative singular, across the intervening words.
Per silvas means 'through the woods'; resonat is the finite verb.
workedExamples.conclusion: 'A loud voice resounds through the woods.' The separated adjective brings its quality forward.

flashcards.front: What is a dactyl's quantity pattern?
Is syllable quantity identical to stress?

diagrams.title: Recovering a separated phrase
diagrams.description: Agreement links words across intervening material.

modules.title: Support an interpretation of epic choice
modules.focus: Unit 5 Vergil: connect action, language and competing obligations.
explanation: An epic character can face obligations that pull in different directions. Analysis should show how a passage presents that conflict through action, speech, imagery or narrative framing. A thematic label such as duty is a starting point; it is not evidence by itself.

Participles and ablative absolutes often compress background circumstances. In the original example “urbe relicta, cives fugerunt”, urbe relicta is an ablative absolute: “After the city had been abandoned, the citizens fled.” Context may support temporal, causal or concessive nuance, but do not add a motive that the grammar alone cannot establish.

workedExample.prompt: Translate “hostibus visis, dux constitit”, an original exercise.
steps: Identify hostibus visis as an ablative absolute: “when the enemies had been seen”.
Translate dux constitit as “the leader stopped”; the sentence does not itself explain whether fear or strategy caused the stop.

misconception.claim: A character’s action proves one fixed motive.
misconception.correction: Motives need support from language and context, and a passage may sustain tension.

questions.prompt: What two components form “urbe relicta” ?
questions.answer: An ablative noun and agreeing perfect passive participle, forming an ablative absolute.
checkpoints: Names both components
Identifies ablative agreement

questions.prompt: How would you support a claim about conflicting obligations?
questions.hint: Move from theme to textual evidence.
questions.answer: Identify two demands in the passage and explain how specific language or actions place them in tension.
checkpoints: Uses two demands
Explains textual support

questions.prompt: Translate the original 'sole oriente, agricolae laborabant'.
questions.answer: The farmers were working as the sun was rising. Sole oriente is an ablative absolute. The present participle makes the rising simultaneous with the work.
checkpoints: The farmers were working as the sun was rising.
Sole oriente is an ablative absolute.
The present participle makes the rising simultaneous with the work.

questions.prompt: A leader leaves after an omen; why is 'the leader is cowardly' not established by sequence alone?
questions.answer: The sequence shows departure after the omen. Fear or cowardice is an interpretation requiring further support. Speech, narrator comment or a pattern of choices could strengthen or challenge that reading.
checkpoints: The sequence shows departure after the omen.
Fear or cowardice is an interpretation requiring further support.
Speech, narrator comment or a pattern of choices could strengthen or challenge that reading.

notes.title: Support an interpretation of epic choice in depth
paragraphs: An ablative absolute typically combines a noun or pronoun in the ablative with a participle, providing a circumstance grammatically separate from the main clause. A perfect passive participle usually places that circumstance before the main action; a present participle commonly makes it simultaneous. Translation may use when, after, because or although if context supports the relationship. The construction alone does not determine a character's moral motive. For an epic interpretation, connect choices to the passage's actual actions, speeches and framing before applying a broad theme such as duty or anger.

workedExamples.prompt: Translate the original 'ponte rupto, milites viam aliam petiverunt'.
steps: Ponte rupto is ablative singular with a perfect passive participle: the bridge having been broken.
The main action is the soldiers seeking another route.
workedExamples.conclusion: 'After the bridge had been broken, the soldiers sought another road.' A deliberate cause of the break is not supplied.

flashcards.front: What does a present participle commonly suggest?
Can the construction alone prove fear?

diagrams.title: Bridge and route
diagrams.description: A prior circumstance frames the soldiers' action.

nodes.label: Blocked passage
nodes.detail: A practical implication supported by context.

modules.title: Prepare a passage-based project argument
modules.focus: Unit 6 project: distinguish translation, context and interpretation.
explanation: A project argument should begin with accurate comprehension of the assigned passages. Record difficult forms, resolve syntax and keep a literal translation beside interpretive notes. A broad historical idea cannot repair a mistranslated verb or an incorrectly identified speaker.

Use contextual sources to clarify the text, while distinguishing established information from your own inference. Organise each claim around a passage feature and explain its effect. The annual project passages are selected for that year; these original exercises do not reproduce them or complete the required project.

workedExample.prompt: Evaluate “The narrator approves because the event is described vividly.”
steps: Identify the unsupported leap: vivid description does not establish approval.
Seek evaluative wording, reported reactions or framing that supports the claimed attitude, and revise the claim if evidence remains ambiguous.

misconception.claim: A fluent English paraphrase proves every Latin detail is understood.
misconception.correction: A paraphrase can conceal errors in tense, agency, negation or reported speech.

questions.prompt: Name two grammatical details to verify before interpreting a passage.
questions.answer: Check the subject or agent and the tense or temporal relationship of the main verbs.
checkpoints: Checks agency
Checks time

questions.prompt: How should a project handle two plausible interpretations?
questions.hint: Compare support rather than forcing certainty.
questions.answer: State the alternatives, weigh the textual evidence and explain why one is stronger or why uncertainty remains.
checkpoints: Uses evidence
Preserves legitimate uncertainty

questions.prompt: Translate the original 'non omnes consilium probaverunt' and state its scope.
hints: Do not turn a partial negative into none.
questions.answer: Not everyone approved the plan. At least some did not approve. The sentence does not say that nobody approved.
checkpoints: Not everyone approved the plan.
At least some did not approve.
The sentence does not say that nobody approved.

questions.prompt: Design a two-column note for an ambiguous passage.
questions.answer: One column records forms, syntax and literal meaning. The other records interpretations with supporting words. Unresolved alternatives remain labelled instead of being presented as settled facts.
checkpoints: One column records forms, syntax and literal meaning.
The other records interpretations with supporting words.
Unresolved alternatives remain labelled instead of being presented as settled facts.

notes.title: Prepare a passage-based project argument in depth
paragraphs: A passage-based argument should keep translation, observation and interpretation distinct. A finite verb's mood or a pronoun's antecedent may change who is responsible for an action, so these details belong in the evidence record. A contextual source can clarify a convention without proving how this particular passage uses it. Compare plausible readings and identify the wording that favours one. An argument is stronger when it states a bounded inference and acknowledges an unresolved grammatical ambiguity than when it substitutes broad historical background for the text's actual relationships.

workedExamples.prompt: Evaluate the original sentence 'cives ducem laudaverunt, sed poeta tacuit' as evidence of unanimous praise.
steps: Translate: 'The citizens praised the leader, but the poet remained silent.'
The adversative sed distinguishes the poet's silence from the citizens' praise.
workedExamples.conclusion: The sentence supports praise by the citizens, not unanimous approval or a certain motive for the poet's silence.

flashcards.front: What should a passage claim cite?
flashcards.back: Specific wording or a grammatical relationship.
Clarify relevant context without replacing textual evidence.

diagrams.title: Testing a universal claim
diagrams.description: One contrast restricts the scope of the conclusion.

nodes.label: Qualified inference
nodes.detail: Praise is documented, unanimity is not.
